title: The island princess, or, The generous Portuguese made into an opera, as it is performed at the Theatre Royal / all the musical entertainments and the greatest part of the play new, and written by Mr. Motteux.
author: Motteux, Peter Anthony, 1660-1718.

segments.head: ACT I. | SCENE I. The Entrance to the Temple in the Palace.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: WE're now in those delicious Eastern Climes
Where ev'ry Wind diffuses balmy sweets.
The Treasure of the Sun dwells here; each Tree,
As if it envy'd the Old Paradice,
Strives to bring forth Immortal Fruit. The Spices,
Renewing Nature, can preserve her Beauties
Untainted in the Grave. The very Rivers as we float along
Throw up their Pearls. The Earth, still cloth'd in Flow'rs,
Teems with the Birth of Gemms, and dazzling Riches:
Nothing that bears a Life but brings a Treasure.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: To wander, with us, Sir, you left betimes
Your Country, tho' the darling of its Court.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: We Portuguese with ease now journey thro' the Globe.
New worlds disclose their Beauties and their Prides to our embraces.
And we the first of Nations find these wonders.
But of 'em all, this Island boasts the greatest;
A Princess whom all Nature's Blessings grace.
The very Sun, I think, respects her Charms;
Nor dares affect 'em with the common gloom.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: So lately Landed, and already struck! Beware, Armusia!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Your Councel comes too late — Let's find the General,
Our Countryman, Ruidias—

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: 'Tis rumour'd, Sir, he loves her.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ha! — Yet I must on, in spight of Reason's Laws,
He meanly loves, whom fancied distance awes;
Like a bright Star, she's fix'd and shines on high,
But Love has wings, and to her Orb I'll fly.

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: You're early here, Piniero.

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: Not so early, Sir.
But I've already seen our Watch reliev'd.
And bid our Guards be careful of their Charge.
The Fort is all our strength in these Spice Islands.

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: And sure our common safety
Requires strict watch upon our Treach'rous Neighbours.

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: Their late attempt is yet too fresh among us,
In which against the Laws of Arms and Nations
The Governor of Ternate seiz'd by stealth
This Island's Monarch, our confederate King,
While for Diversion coasting in his Barge.

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: His Royal Sister, the admir'd Quisara,
Has shew'd a noble mind, and tender'st Love
To her unhappy Brother and the nobler
Because his Fall wou'd raise her to a Throne.

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: Such Charms and Virtue with just admiration
Have robb'd the Neighbou^ng Courts, and fill'd her
Palace with Royal Suiters —
Our General is in among 'em too, and has the start, 'tis thought.

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: But have you seen Armusia,
The handsome Portuguese arriv'd here lately?
I fear he'll spoil his game, Piniero.

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: A Man of noble Promise,
Without Reserv'dness Grave, and doubtless Valiant,
For he that dares come hither dares fight any where.
But hold —
We're in the Palace of the Island,
Not our own Fort. D'ye mark these Preparations?
Those doors lead to the Temple, where the Princess
Has summon'd all her Lovers to assemble;
But to what Purpose we are yet to learn.

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: But who are chief?

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: That swelling vanity, the King of Bakam.
The next Syana's Prince; but, what's the greatest wonder,
The haughty Governor, our Enemy,
He that surprized the King, to gain the Sister,
Is under formal Hostages arriv'd. —

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: You're welcome, to Tidore, Sir!
Know there is nothing in our power to serve you,
But you may freely challenge.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Sir, we thank you, and rest your Servants.

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: Brave Armusia, you never saw this Court before—
But hark, the Signal's given, and see the Pageants enter.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: These sure are Islanders.

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: And Princes.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What may he be that bears so proud a Port?

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: The King of Bakam, Sir, a mere Barbarian —
This is Syana's Prince — and that the Governour
Who seiz'd the King, and keeps him Prisoner.—

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Away, ye Trifles;
Am I in Competition with such Toys!

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: You speak loud, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Young man, I will speak louder.
Can any man but I deserve her favour?
Ye petty Princes!

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Thou proud vain Thing, whom Nature —

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: I contemn Thee, and that Fort-keeping Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Keep thy Rank, Thing, with thy own petty Peers—
Call out the Princess?

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Dost thou know me, Bladder?
Art thou acquainted with my Nature?
What can'st thou merit?

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Merit! I'm above it.
Honour's my Servant, Fortune is my Slave.
I slight ye, Insects: had not the vain People
Bestowed some Titles on ye, I shou'd forget your Names.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Sir, talk less, that men may think you can do more.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Why, I can talk and do.
I tell you, only I deserve the Princess,
And make good, only I, if you dare, you,
Or you, Syana's Prince.—

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Here lies my Proof.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: I'll be short with you.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: For shame forbear, ye Princes; rule your angers:
You violate the Freedom of this Place,
The State and Royalty—

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: He's well content I see, so I have done.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: You wrong me, and my Court, contentious Princes.
Comes your Love drest in violence to seek us?
Is't fit our Palace, and this Sacred Place
Shou'd be polluted with your bloody Rage?
He that loves me, loves my Commands; be temperate,
Or be no more what you profess, my Servants.

speeches.speaker: Omn.
verse: We are calm as Peace.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What Command she carries,
And what a sparkling Majesty flies from her!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Since you're for Action, I shall find you danger:
But not this way: 'Tis not this mean Contention
Among your selves, nor Courtship to my Face
Who best can Love, or who can flatter most
Shall guide my choice; he that will hope my Favour
Must win me with his merit.

speeches.speaker: Omn.
verse: Propose the way.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: First I shall call our Gods to witness what I promise.
Now give me hearing. 'Tis well known to you,
The King my Brother is Pris'ner to this Man.
Were I Ambitious there I'd let him die;
And wear his Crown; but greatness cannot tempt me
To forget Nature, and a King's Distress.
Therefore the Man that wou'd be known my Lover
Must first redeem my Brother, or seek another Mistress.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Divine Creature!

speeches.speaker: Chri.
verse: A dang'rous task; how they stand gazing all!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I grant ye, this will be no easie work,
But the Reward is certain—Ruidias cold!
Perhaps you doubt me, Princes.
He that shall free the King, shall be my Husband.
By that most bright and Sacred Shrine, I swear,
Before these Holy Men I here proclaim it.
No stirring yet?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: If, Madam, to attempt this Royal Rescue
Thro' all forms of Danger
Might crown your hope, I had not lost this Minute;
But here, where Conduct must keep Pace with Courage,
The starting fiery Will is rein'd with Torment
To Judgment's flower march.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Take your own Method.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Madam, believe him here. I'll raise an Army,
Shall bring him to you, Island, Fort and all,
And fix it here.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: What may be, Madam,
And what my Pow'r can promise, I engage.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Ha; Ha!
Madam, their Pow'r and Arts are all too weak,
'Tis only in my Will to give your Wishes.
I seiz'd your Brother to secure you mine.
Then thus the Treaty's finisht! Take your Prisoner,
And make me yours, close Prisoner to these Arms:
Say but the word, your Brother shall be render'd quick as your wishes.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Know, base Ravisher,
I hate both you, your Country, and your Love.
Heav'n knows how dear I prize his Liberty;
But e're I wou'd so basely buy his Freedom,
I'd study to forget he was my Brother.
By Force you took him; he that wou'd possess me,
Must fetch him back by Force, or ne're succeed.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Noble Spirit!

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Be Wise, and use me better.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I say by Force, and suddenly— so return, Sir;
And glad we have kept Faith for your safe Passage.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: Your hopes are great, good Governor.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Am I then made a Property?
I'll check this Pride. This neglect of me
Shall cost your Brother dear.
For, as till now I've us'd him like a King,
He now shall in a Dungeon fetter'd lye,
Darkness and lingring Death for his Companions.
And let me see who dares attempt his Rescue.
Farewell: And when you find him thus, lament your scorn.
Nay, I shall make you kneel to take my Offer.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Provoking Insolence! he dares you, Princes.
Your Honour now's concern'd. Haste, joyn your Powers;
When Majesty's thus wrong'd all Princes shou'd revenge.
Oh that I were a Man to lead you on,
To free a King, and punish that Barbarian,
That Tyrant, who by treach'rous Force wou'd gain
What ev'n submissive Truth can scarce obtain.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: We must resolve and speedily. Walk with me Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Now, Sir, you stand as you were charm'd.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: O Sosa, O Emanuel!

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: What now?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: This Captive King! What an Action
Would this be to put forwards, Friends! What glory

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: And what an everlasting Wealth to crown it!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To step into't while they are thinking.

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: Sir, 'tis impossible; The Fort's impregnable.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: No more, dissuade me not, for I will rule in this.

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: If it must be —

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Stay not for second Thoughts—Oh! She's an Angel!
At least we can attempt; our very Fate
Will sometimes be the Theme of her Discourse,
And I would dye ten thousand thousand Deaths
To have her talk of me—
Love, Love with all his Fires has shot himself
Into my Soul, and urges on to dare.
Shou'd we succeed, how vast is the Reward!
Come on, my Friends! — For such a Prize 'tis wise to hazard all;
Blest if we Live, and Glorious tho' we Fall.

segments.head: ACT II. | SCENE I. A Vault under the Castle.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: OUR prosperous Passage was a lucky Omen,
The Sea and Wind strove which should most befriend us.
Where lies our Boat?

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: Safe lodg'd within the Reeds behind the Enemies Castle.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: These Merchant's Habits too have done us service:
Unquestion'd thus I've travel'd thro the Town,
View'd all the Tyrant's Magazines; got knowledge
Ev'n of the Prison,
Where the King's dungeon'd, and the Power that guards it.

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: You attempt strong Work.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Courage is strong; besides a Monarch's Fate's in't;
Yet lose or win, there's no retiring now.
Thus far our Game holds fair, as Merchants we
Have hir'd this Vault, and stow'd those Mattled Wares,
That soon will blow it up.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: The Trains are laid, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Come nearer then,
That no false Ear may reach us; o're this Vault
The Castle stands, where the proud Governor
Has stor'd his Arms and Treasure, next to that
The Prison where the injur'd King is kept.
The Fire I've brought shall break out into Flames
That all the Island shall stand wond'ring at.
When the Town's full of Fright, and all employ'd
To quench the Flames, then fly we to the Prison,
And push for the King's Rescue.

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: Fortune speed us!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Let us be worthy of it by our Courage,
And so take leave, but keep still within sight,
Till the Flames rise, then meet to do or dye.
Fail not, dear Fire, and Powder, hold your Nature;
By useful Mischiefs nobly triumph here!
Redeem a King, and serve a matchless Fair,
Assist my Love, and make one happy Pair.

segments.head: ACT II. | Scene the Town of Ternate.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: No, Captain, for those Troops, we need 'em not,
The Town is strong enough to stand their Furies.
D'you think they dare attempt to free the King?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Perhaps by Treaty,
But sure by Force they will not prove so forward.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Well, wou'd I had the Princ^ss, I must have her,
In spight of all her scorn. — Hark! what's that?
That Noise there, it went with a violence.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Some Wall, belike, Sir, is fallen suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Fire, Fire!

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I hear another Tune, 'tis loud and dreadful.
Look up into the Town, how bright the Air shews!
Upon my Life some sudden Fire — The Bell too.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: Fire, Fire!

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Where? Where?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: Suddenly taken in a Merchant's Vault, Sir,
It blazes fearfully! help! help, good People.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Your Magazine's a fire, Sir, help, help, suddenly,
All will be lost.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Raise all the Garrison.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: The Flames increase! help, help dear Citizens.
Freedom and Wealth to him that helps!
Fling Wine, fling any Thing, I'll see it recompens'd.
Fire, Fire! What, my Brats hanging still about me! get you gone, you young Bastards, go, go and plunder!
I heard 'em cry Fire, I wish I knew where 'tis, I'm deadly cold.
Oh Neighbour, run, save your Goods, your House is a Fire.
I don't care, I've got the Key in my Pocket.

segments.head: ACT II. | SCENE changes to a Prison, and a prospect of Fire.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: So, thou art open, keep the Way clear behind still,
Now for the place where the King lies.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: 'Tis here, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Force open the Door; quick, while the Guards are scatter'd.
All's in disorder — The Fire rages on—
Oh 'tis a glorious blaze— Ha! a miserable object!
Yet by his manly Face he shows a King.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Why stare ye on me?
You cannot put on Faces to fright me:
In death, I'm still a King.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Quick, break the Chain!
Oh Barb'rous Wretches thus to use a Prince.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What does this mean?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Sir, we are Friends, and come to set you free!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Heaven! thou art gracious.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ha! the Guard! Charge 'em!
They fly! the day is ours! the King is free.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Thou gen'rous stranger, what art thou! Some Angel sure.
Oh! if thou art a man, let me embrace thee?
Command my Pow'r, my Life.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Your Love, no more, Sir.
But now let's hence! haste to the Boat,
Then to Tidore, there, there is my Reward.
Such a Reward! Oh the thoughts on't transport me.
Possess'd of that, I shall think India poor.
There is no Wealth but she: She's Crowns, and Scepters,
Health, Freedom, Life, the Empire of the Globe;
Nay, more, she's—she's the Woman I adore,
And with Armusia that outweighs the World.
What, is the Fire out, or past the worst yet?

'Tis out, Neighbour, but whether past the worst or no, I know not. I never so bestirr'd my self since I was a Man. I have been burnt at both ends like a Squib. I liv'd two long hours in the Fire. The Flame at last got down into my Throat, and broke out again I don't know where. I fry'd like a burnt Marrow-Bone..—If they had not clap'd in a dozen Buckets on this goodly Tenement of mine, I had flam'd up like any Tavern Brush, and been one of the seven Stars by this Time.
Well, of all the seven Elements, ware fire, say I.

Seven Elements, quoke he! why, you talk as if the Fire had scar'd you out of your seven Sences! I tell ye there are but four Elements: Water and Malt are two of 'em; and Fire and Brimstone, the other. They've past thro' me a little too lately, I thank 'em.
Hold, I say, there's a fifth Element, right Brandy.
Thou art drunk?
Right then, now I'm in my Element.
Ay, Neighbour, if ev'ry Man had wrought as you did.

Why, I stole nothing, you slandring Cuckold you. That Son of a Batchelor is always back-biting a man to his face. I'd have you to know, I scorn your words. 'Tis well known I get my living at my Finger's ends, and that too I get out of the Fire, as a man may say.
How many Rogues were there pretending to help remove Goods, and ran away with 'em.
Ay, those unconscionable Rogues! I hate 'em. I hate a Thief.
But is there not a deal of damage done?

Only some six score houses burnt, that's all, Neighbour — Come let's go home, and fright our Wives, for we look like Devils! away! yonder comes our Governor, a worse Plague than the Fire, he has beams enough yet standing to hang us all.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Fool'd with a Fire! Oh I cou'd tear my Limbs.
The King is scap'd, fled, past Recovery,
All, all my hopes of Love and Greatness lost.
Shall I give over then? No, Spight, Ambition,
Revenge, and fiercer Love forbid it. Rather,
I'll venture all, and, in disguise, unknown,
Crown my Foe's Fortune, or retrieve my own.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Love bids me dare, but reason bids delay.
Our strength is now too small for such a Siege.
Yet I must on, the Princess Fires my Soul,
And though she seems to favour my addresses
Unless I free the King I must despair.
Well then, I'll die, or do't — We'll now embark —
What means that Shout?

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: Where are you, Sir? Oh you're undone, prevented.
The King's releas'd, he's coming in his Barge,
That met him nigh the Port.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Impossible! who should redeem him?
The Princes are all here.

speeches.speaker: Pini.
verse: 'Tis done, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: It cannot be! Done! who dares do it?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Can it be possible! The King returning!
Freed by a Stranger! Oh my Fatal Vow!

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Grief strikes me dumb!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I thought none but Ruidias cou'd have freed him.
Is there another like him in the World?
But Oh! Surprise and Grief betray me, and I lose
The Sister's gladness in the Lover's sorrow.
Oh Brother! cou'd I have thought I shou'd have shed a Tear
For your Return, unless it were for Joy!

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Oh Princess!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: The general Joy comes on,
And I must meet it, but oh with what comfort?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Rise my Sister!
I am not welcome yet, till you embrace me.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: My Royal Brother! Oh I'm lost in Pleasure,
To see you safe again.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Sir, I rejoyce to see you here restor'd,
But must repine, that 'twas not by my means:
'Twas a brave Deed, I envy him that did it:
Yet had it mist, my project had not fail'd.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I thank you, noble Sir, I know you love me.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: I have an Army, Sir,
That wou'd have scour'd your Tyrant and his Country.
I'm sorry you're releas^d, and wish you in your Dungeon again,
That I might bring you hither at my Armies Head.

speeches.speaker: Sya.
verse: I have done nothing, Sir, and therefore think it
Convenient to say little of what my Love design'd.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I like your Modesty — My gen^rous Friends,
I thank you all; I know it griev'd ye
To hear my Misery: But this Man, Princes,
I must thank heartily indeed.
This wondrous Man, even from the Grave of Sorrow,
Has rais'd me up to Freedom, Life, and Empire.
Oh Sister, if there may be thanks for this,
Or any thing near Recompense, invent it.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You are too Noble Sir, there is Reward,
Reward above my Action too, by Millions;
A Recompense, so Rich, so Great, so Glorious
I du^st not dream it mine, but that .twas promis'd
Before the Face of Heaven.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O speak it, speak it, bless me with the Knowledge.
Make me a happy man,
For still methinks I am a Prisoner,
And feel no Liberty, till that is found.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: It is— (But first to Heav'n and you I bend;
If either can forgive the high Demand)
It is your Sister, Royal Sir, She's mine.
I claim her, by her own Word, and her Honour:
It was her open Promise to the Man
That durst redeem you—Beauty set me on,
And Fortune crowns my hopes, if She receive me.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Receive you, Sir—Why, Sister! ha! turn from him?
Stand as you knew not me, nor what he has ventur'd?
My dearest Sister!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: O Sir, your Pardon,
There is a blushing Modesty
That holds her back; Virgins are nice to Love;
I wou'd not have her forc'd; give her fair liberty:
Ladies of her soft Nature, if compell'd,
Turn into Fears, and fly ev'n their own Wishes.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Look on him, Princess, is there such another?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Sir, I confess,
My Word is pass'd, and he by that has purchas'd;
But yet be pleas'd to give me Time to be
Acquainted with his Merit: we are Strangers,
And Love, like Pow'r, must pass thro Ceremonies,
E're it can fix in Virgin's hearts.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Be speedy.
You will respect your Word: I know you will:
I'll be your Pledge, my Hero: Come, my Sister,
Let's see what Welcome you can give a Prisoner,
And what kind Looks a Friend —
Thus in my Arms once more.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You make me blush, Sir.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Let this Day see our whole Court crown'd with Pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Leveridge. Shepherd.
verse: This glorious Day, let Pleasures flow;
Now Love and Hymen jar no more:
Ye Sports, appear, let Sorrow cease below;
Hither repair, the Golden Age restore:
Let Mortals share the Blessings of the Skies.
See Jove for ever cease to rove,
And own, tho' Nuptial Fewds arise,
No Joys can Vye with Lawful Love.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Freeman. A Shepherd.
verse: Happy he who wisely chose
To taste of Love without his Woes.
"Happy She whose Charms improve
"The soft Delights of Harmless Love.

speeches.speaker: CHORUS.
verse: Change may raise a wanton Fire,
But Truth can best improve Desire,
And Kindles, never to expire.

speeches.speaker: M. Pate and Mr. Leveridge. Two Shepherds.
verse: Cease, ye Rovers, cease to Range
Pleasure revels least in Change.
Wandring still, and still uneasy,
Nought can fix ye, nought can please ye;
While True Love, like Heav'nly Joys,
Never dies, and never cloys.

speeches.speaker: A Shepherdess.
verse: "From drooping Minds let Sorrow fly,
"Joy must reign, and Anguish die.
"Souls who grieve for Coy Denying,
"Hearts now raging, Wretches dying,
"Know, that Lovers who pursue,
"Soon or late the Fair subdue.
"Blame your Fear when you despair,
"Not the wishing dying Fair.

speeches.speaker: Mr. Magnus's Boy. A Shepherd.
verse: All the Pleasures, Hymen brings
Lawful Sweets, and chast Desires,
All the Pleasures Hymen brings,
Flow from ever-living Springs,
And never-dying Fires.

speeches.speaker: Mis Lindsey. A Shepherdess.
verse: The Jolly Swains
That were roving o're the Plains
From all Regions hither fly,
To claim kind Hymen's gentle Tye.
With their wanton Motions courting
Some lovely Maid
Whose Eyes persuade
To soft Delights, and am'rous Sporting.

speeches.speaker: Grand CHORUS.
verse: Love's Flame divinely burns:
The Golden Age returns.
Jove, Juno, and Cupid, and Hymen agree,
All Hearts thus are bless'd, and less happy when free.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Lead on! Sister, your hand to my Deliverer.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh let me first approach it with a Kiss,
Thus trembling with Extremity of Bliss.
Wisely, bright Princess, you allay the Joy,
Still slowly Bless, and leasurely Destroy.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: SIR, why so sad amidst so much good Fortune?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I want what Beggars are allow'd, Content.

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: Does then the King neglect you?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: No, he is grateful ev'n to meer profuseness,
But Oh his Sister, that disdainful Fair,
That shou'd a little smile upon my service,
And foster my Deserts, with care avoids me,
Spight of her solemn Promise.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: And you go sighing up and down for this?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What would you have me do?

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Do what a Man that knows the Sex wou'd do
In such a Case, go to her.

speeches.speaker: So.
verse: That's the way.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: And talk as if you fought for her, boldly.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I shall do something; but with more Respect.
Pray leave me to my Thoughts, and in an hour command me.
What shall I do to move her Soul to Pity!
Ha! This Woman waits on her—Lower I cannot fall,
I'll try my Fate—Madam, May I presume—

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: 'Tis the brave stranger! a handsome Gentleman!
How happy will she be in such a Husband!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You wait on the Princess;
With one kind Office you may bind a Gentleman
Hereafter to be yours. Such beauteous Faces
Shou'd have courteous minds.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Tell me your Business, Sir.
Yet if it be to her, I think your self
Wou'd do much better, I know your Interest.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I want assurance,
And am yet but a Stranger — I wou'd speak with her^punc;

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: She's now alone.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Pray wear this, and believe my meaning civil—
I wou'd speak to her in private.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: You shall, Sir.
Be pleased to go with me;
My Chamber's next to her's. But pray be secret.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: As Death.

segments.head: ACT. III. The Palace. | SCENE II.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: So far and truly you've discover'd to me
The former Currents of my Life and Fortunes
That I acknowledge you most Wise and Holy,
And credit your Predictions.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: I have liv'd long sequester'd from the World
To find out Knowledge, which I've now attain'd to.
Many a Mystic Vision have I seen
Wherein the good and evils of these Islands
Were lively shadow'd. Many a Charge I've had too,
Still as the Time grew ripe, to reveal these,
And now I speak.
Beware these Portuguese!
The Cause is now the Gods: hear and believe. King!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I do, but know I've found 'em gentle, faithful,
And am oblig'd to 'em for my Deliverance.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: O Son, the Aims of Men are to be look'd at
Above their present actions:
These Men came hither, as my vision tells me,
Almost starv'd, and Shipwrackt, begg'd leave to Trade,
Grew rich, then suck'd the Fat,
And Freedom of this Isle, taught her to tremble,
Witness the Fort they've clapt here on the Neck
Of your Tidore.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: They have so, indeed, Father.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Take heed! your late delivery is only
A fair fac'd Prologue to future mischief.
Mark but the end of your Restorer!
Your Sister is his due. What's she? your Heir, Sir.
And what's he akin then to the Kingdom?
But Heirs are not ambitious — who thou suffers?
What reverence shall our Gods have? And what Justice
The miserable People?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You've well advis'd me.
And I will seriously consider, Father.
In the mean time you shall have fair access
To my Sister, dispose her to your Purpose,
And let me still know how the Gods determine.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: So, thanks to this false Beard, and falser Cant,
I've hopes to ruin thee, and my bold Rival.
The Bramins shall foment the Pious mischief;
And when each Party's weaken'd, I'll unmask,
Strike in between, and get the Princess and the Crown.
Revive my hopes! Revive! — Mankind to fool,
Still the great Maxim is; divide and rule.

segments.head: ACT. III. The Palace. | SCENE III, The Princesses Apartment.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Sing me a Song, then leave me—and if Ruidias
Sould come and beg admittance, introduce him.
But stay—Will Vertue warrant this admission?
Surely, for once it may, in such an Exigence —
We must consult about this Turn of Fortune.
Lovely Charmer, dearest Creature,
Kind Invader of my heart,
Grac'd with ev'ry gift of Nature,
Rais'd with ev'ry grace of Art!
Oh! cou'd I but make thee love me,
As thy Charms my heart have mov'd,
None cou'd e're be blest above me,
None cou'd e're be more belov'd.
Shield me, ye Powers! What's here!
Sure 'tis the Phantasm of the Man I dread,
Form'd by my Fears! Who are you?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: The fondest and most wretched of your slaves.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Who waits there? Rude Intruder, leave me.
What means this Treachery? Who let you in?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What cou'd keep out the Love that brought me hither.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: This is an Insolence unparalell'd,
Nor shall my Brother's Love protect this boldness.
I'm mistress of my self, and will not be
Thus visited, spight of your boasted Service.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Bright Vertue —

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Stand off, I read dishonour in your Eyes.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: By all that Beauty they are Innocent.
Pray tremble not, you have no Cause, Fair Princess.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: So base a violation of my Privacy!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: If vertuous Love may claim a pitying glance,
Look on me, and believe me! Is this violence?
Far be it from my heart to fright your quiet,
And heaviest curse falls on him that intends it;
If you mistrust me still, take this and sheath it here.
'Twill give a Wound less cruel than your doubts.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Why this Intrusion then?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: With trembling aw to urge my Love and Service.
But hopes remove, the nearer I approach you,
And I even dread to claim what you have promised.
So much more easie was the task proposed
Than to demand the Recompence. Oh Princess!
When greatness check'd the Fire your Beauty kindled,
Your promise fann'd it to a Flame. I dar'd,
But 'twas you quicken'd hope: Then kill it not;
My flame is grown too mighty to be quench'd;
Yet Oh, 'tis pure, 'tis free from selfish dross.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: May I believe?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Wrong not your Charms that claim no less a duty.
Believe me all devoted to your Will.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh, Love! Why must I be ungrateful to such merit.
Shall I exact a Proof of your Obedience?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Command a thousand, till I've tir'd your doubts
Set any task, Mortality may dare.
Point out new dangers, bid me Face Destruction.
Command me any thing — but not to Love.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Then hear me! Cease for ever to expect
The Recompence you ask'd, and leave me now.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What have I promis'd?
Is this my doom, and is there no redress?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: But one, which you must to my pity owe,
For I must blush to tell your Cure— I love—
My heart was all dispos'd before you claim'd it.
Fancy had got the start of your deserts,
Which yet I prize so high, that for your Ease
I force my modesty on this Confession,
To disengage your hopes, nor let the man
That has so highly serv'd, depend on fruitless air.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh, Madam!—

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Replies are vain: Obey!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Wretched Armusia. Doubly wretched now;
What wilt thou do? Can'st thou resign thy Princess?
Resign her to a Rival? Tamely yield
Thy beauteous Prize, and starve thy self to let
Another Riot. Oh this Racks my Soul!
Grief, Jealous Rage, Despair, and Envy tear it.
Bid me with naked Brest go storm a Breach,
When thro' the dreadful gap a thousand Deaths,
Rush down in Fires and Rocks and Iron hail.
But change th' ungrateful task. 'Tis death to hope,
And hope's the Life of Love; 'tis torment in extream,
Wheels, Daggers, dying Pangs, and lingring Fires.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Hard fate! Why must I use him thus? But Oh!
I must be cruel to my self or him,

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Still dumb, relentless Fair? Well, I'll content you,
And keep my Promise, tho' I lose my Life.
Despair will make that easie, Joy attend you,
While I withdraw to die; It should be at your Feet,
But I will not Prophane this Place, nor cost
Your heart a sigh, Farewel!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Stay, gen'rous Stranger: your despair alarms me,
Oh, promise me to live.
See, see the Pity which I pay your anguish:
My grateful Soul suffers no less than yours;
For 'tis a pain to be so much oblig'd
And Bankrupt in Returns. It kills my Joy,
I'm angry with my self, and torn in two.
I wou'd recall my heart, but Oh! I cannot. Fear, Duty,
Honour, Shame, Pity, Gratitude and Love distract me,
War in my Brest, my Head, my Soul, and strain the strings of Life.
Oh leave, leave me, my Confusion is such,
I dread to say too little or too much.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh stay;

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I cannot; must not.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Must I then leave you thus? Oh! if I must,
First see th' affliction of my Soul, see now a separation
More cruel more a death
Than that between the Body and the Soul:
They part to meet again, to be more bless'd;
But I to be divorc'd from Joy for ever.
Let me be mad, ye Powers, or let me die!
Oh Heavens! Oh Princess, Judge what I endure,
When Death or Madness must bestow the Cure.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Ha! who is this?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Who art thou?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: My Rival with the Princess! and so private.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ha! 'Tis Ruidias,
My happy Rival,
But hold out, Patience, yet!

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Is there not door enough, you take such elbow room.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What I take I'll carry.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Confusion. Know proud man, I love the Princess; she harkens to my suit,
And tho in Portugal you claim precedence,
I.ll have it here; here I command the Fort,
And that commands the Town. Be wise, desist,
Or with my Sword —

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You wou'd not use it here?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh hold! — Ruidias, you I may command,
Forbear, and as you prize my Love, respect him.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Is then his Life so dear to you? I'm lost.
Had I your leave to wait on you, and for this?
Oh I've not Patience. Must I be outdone?
Out brav'd, out rival.d? Must that Stranger get
At once the start in Glory and in Love,
And tread me like a name in sand, to nothing?
Death, and Hell! shall I bear it? tamely bear it?
No, e re I do, I'll give or take a Life.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Brave stranger, by your Love I charge you,
Retire, and entertain no thoughts of Vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: O my Patience!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: 'Tis with you still: Oh do not chide it from you.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Weak flesh rebels, but you and Vertue Conquer.
I go, but judge, Oh judge! ye tender hearts,
What Pangs, what Racks the wretched Lover tear
Who to his Rival leaves the darling fair.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Great soul, I am asham'd I cannot love him yet.
Now, you, whose Jealous Rage is so presumptuous,
Know, I resent it and your disrespect.
Your Love stands yet upon my Courtesie:
'Tis true, I've suffer'd you to tell your Passion,
But I ne're promis'd you a kind return;
And if you dare abuse your privilege—

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Armusia here, and stealing out, when I
Had hopes to be in private entertain'd!
What Lover cou'd have tamely born the sight?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Know what I am? how durst you doubt my honour?
I never taught you to dispose my Freedom;
And had I promis'd you my heart, 'twere a less Crime
In me to change than in you to suspect me;
The first's but frailty, but the last ill Nature.
Is this your Faith? True Love is more respectful.
Armusia wou'd not pass so rash a Censure;
And I shou'd punish thee; I'll strive to do't.
'Tis still the Lot of groundless Jealousie
To bring on what it fears.
Vows, Duty, Gratitude concur to exclude thee,
Yet should I slight thee, should I chuse thy Rival
Blame most thy self, and learn how dang'rous 'tis
To let a Woman, spight of Wisdom's Laws,
See that you're Jealous, tho' without a Cause.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: She's gone! what shall I do? Oh that Armusia
Hangs betwixt hopes and me, and threats my Ruin:
He has her vows, fresh Services, the King,
And a vast stock of merit on his side:
I have but naked Love, and wav'ring too, I fear.
The Sword then in my hand, I now must try
To fix my Fortune, and o'recome, or die:
When Conquest can't by formal means be got,
A brave Despair may cut the Gordian knot.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: HOld, John, e're you leave me, i'troth I will know
Whither so smugg'd up thus early you go?
With clean Hands and Face,
Your best Band with a Lace,
Your Sunday Reparel when you shou'd go Plough,
So trim none wou'd think you a married Man now.
Hold, John, e're you leave me, itroth I will know
Whither so smugg'd up thus early you go?

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Go, Joan, I wo'n't tell you: To lead a sweet Life
I've learnt of my Betters to steal from my Wife.
Mayhaps with my Neighbour I'll dust it away,
Mayhaps play at Put, or some other such Play.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I guess at what game you'd be playing to day.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Don't plague me. The Devil's in Women I think.
Go, Joan, I tell thee I'm going to drink?
Come, prithee, don't think that I've got no more Grace:
Nay go, or I'll gi^ thee a Dowse in the Face.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I'll find then some body to strike in your Place.
Why should you deny me? I never did you.
Because I an't new, you won't give me my due,
But Troth if you wo'not, another shall do.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: If thus you e're do,
Oh! how I'll belabour your Booby and you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: If thus you e're do,
Oh how I'll belabour your Trollop and You.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse:
Oh how I'll belabour

your Booby and you
your Trollop and you, and you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Well, John, do not go,
And I wo'not do so,
Do not go, my dear Johny,
My Precious, my Hony.
Oh pray do not go,
And I wo'not do so.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Adsooks by that Buss I'm inveigled to stay,
Come, Joan, come and spoil me from going astray.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Come give your best Band.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Here take my best Band.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: Now, give me thy Hand.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Thus 'tis with you Women.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Thus 'tis with you Men.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: Whene're you fall out 'tis to fall in again.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: In vain with Mirth you wou'd beguile my Cares.
Alas! I'm dead to Joy, and but a walking Trouble,
Insensible to all but Love and Grief,
To all but Grief, for Grief and Love are one.
Why wou'd my Rival kill me? If he hates me
Sure he shou'd bid me live! — Let's range the Grove
Perhaps I soon shall meet him, or my Princess.
Both can deal Death; yet I, like other Wretches,
Tho! that's my only Ease, must struggle with my Fate.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: I wou'd talk further with you from the Gods.
You are a Princess of that Excellence—
Nay do not blush, I do not flatter you.
The Gods bestow'd this on you.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I own their Bounty.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Apply it then to their Use, to their Honour,
To ruine or convert those Misbelievers
Those Portuguese; Invite 'em to our Temples—

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Father we may sit yonder, and be still more private.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: What, did Armusia then return the Challenge
You carried him? Will he not meet me?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: He calmly told me, that he disapproves
All formal Duels, yet that with a Sword
He ev'ry Day is walking in this Grove.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Then let us strive to find him out — But see he comes.
Now Love, Revenge, and Fortune guide my Arm.
Draw, Armusia!
Dye or resign the Princess.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I will do neither.
But hold, why must our Friends now share our Danger?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Stand still, I charge ye, as you honour me.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: And, good Emanuel, hold—

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: 'Tis well you spoke—

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Fight home, I will not spare you,
Nor do I look for mercy.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Ha! fighting! hold! Oh hold, rash Men! Oh part 'em!

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Let 'em alone, let 'em kill one another.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Ruidias, hold.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Unless he dyes, I'm hopeless.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: If e're you lov'd, I charge ye cease! Oh! Father.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: My Love were small, shou'd I desist.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Oh let both fall, kind Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Ruidias down!

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Stand still, or my Sword's in—

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh hold Armusia.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: I can expect no Mercy. Why do you not kill me then?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: A Boy might do as much at this Advantage.
Will you not ask your Life?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: 'Tis not worth asking.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Nor is it worth my taking in this Posture.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Spare him Armusia, spare him.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: My Love is all Obedience. Rise, Sir, and take your Sword again

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Not against him that spar'd me! Oh curst Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: What have you done? 'Twere better they had all perish'd.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Father, be pacify'd; I'm working for the best—
This Jealous Rage and Disobedience cure me —
Armusia, meet me in the Neighbouring Temple.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Madam, I shall—
Come brave Ruidias, let us now be Friends;
Believe your Honor safe.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Oh you have beat me both ways, and so nobly
That I must ever love the hand that did it.
But Oh the Princess. Both cannot possess her.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: You cannot, Sir, unless She break her Vow.
Come leave these Toys; and wed your Mistress, Fame.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh Sir, you ask too too much of a Lover.
Ev'n I my self had rather leave the world, than quit so fair a Prize.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: And you alone deserve her. Yet, Armusia,
I cannot yet resign her, tho' I must.
The heat of Love remains, tho' the Soul hope is fled.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Yet let's be Friends. Why shou'd we hate each other
For Sympathy in Love?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Too gen'rous Man, I cannot call you Rival,
Let me embrace you; Let all hatred end.
Oh thus I'm blest—What e're the Fates intend,
I cannot lose, possest of such a Friend.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: I need not now repeat what we've to dread
From these bold mis-believing Portuguese.
Therefore to ruine them, all means are just.
Thus I've decoy'd to Princess the invite
Her promis'd Husband hither, where no doubt
He will Blaspheme our Gods.
The King will in Disguise hear their Discourse.
You know your Time t'appear and back my words.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: You need not doubt us in so good a Cause

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: See, Madam, at your Feet your faithful Slave
Who studies new humility to please you,
And takes a kind of Joy in his afflictions, because they come from you.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh rise, Sir, I did not invite you hither
Thus to prophane our Altars, but to ask
A better Proof of Love than so misplac'd a Worship;
A Proof wh^en, since I've sworn, since you persist,
Must make me yours, at least my grateful Duty.
Few Brides, alas! at first have more to give.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh name it, Madam, what wou'd I not do,
Tho' but to gain you thus: Love, greedy Love,
That still unsatisfy'd, still murm'ring Passion
Will pine, but since 'tis often but Esteem
And gratitude improv'd, 'twill shoot at last
Forc'd by a Zeal like mine. Oh then command me.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Now harken, Sir, and as he treats our Gods
So use him, or expect severest Judgments.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Change your Religion, and adore our Gods.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Renounce-your Faith.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Heav'n forbid!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Offer as we do?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To Wood and Stone, vile Beasts, and cursed Devils?
Is this the Proof you ask?

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: O Blasphemy!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Peace.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I'll reason with you. Are not our Gods as great as yours?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: They are senceless, wretched, and the worst of Creatures,
Unfit to help themselves, much less mankind.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: The Sun and Moon we worship, they are heavenly.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: But I the Maker of that Sun and Moon
Who gave 'em Motion, Influence, and Light.
Excuse me, Princess, if my Zeal for Truth
Extort a gen'rous Freedom of my Tongue.
You shou'd have said, Instruct the King and me.
In that blest Doctrine that guides Souls to Heaven.
Oh may you follow that, destroy your Idols,
Beat down their Altars, ruine their false Temples—

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Oh horror! My Prophecy was true.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I'm sorry I came hither—I've heard too much.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Thus far in Charity I was oblig'd
To rectifie the Errors of your Thought,
Nor can the Blame be mine to want success.
'Twas by these Gods that I was sworn to wed you
These upon blaspheme: You have renounc'd their Power
And thereby free me from all obligation.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You are too just to make this slight Evasion.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: You shall both find me just, sincere and plain
Therefore resolve to quit your Faith or me.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: My Life is yours, but my Religion Heavens
And I no more can change it than my Love.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: You hear your Task.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh! Princess, cease t'injoyn what heav'n forbids.
Name any Task that Honour may not blush
To execute, Toyls, Dangers, Death it self,
But do not, do not tempt me to be bad.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Obey, and instantly; or from this hour
No Recantation shall prevail.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Call you this Charity?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Nay then—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You must not go.
What have I done, to merit this hard Sentence?
To have my very Soul rack'd, forc'd to quit
My Heav'n above, or Paradice on Earth!
How well I love, how much I prize your Charms
My Life must show, but Honour, Conscience, Heaven
I never must forego. Must I then lose You or my self?
Can You persist? Must I be torn from you? I must —
Yet once more let me gaze — O now I cannot go.
Dreadful Strife! Cruel Struggle.
I must not look, nor leave her!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Farewel.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Stay, stay, dear Mischief! — But what am I doing?
Ha! — Now I dread my Thoughts—assist, ye Pow'rs!
Awake my Soul! Oh look no more my Eyes.
Hush! Treacherous Love!
Since Heart or Soul must perish on this Sea
Sink thou, my Heart, to save the immortal Treasure.
Quit thy rich Claim, tho' while I so resign,
No Martyrdom sure ever equal'd mine.
Away, away! Oh! If I look I dye,
There's no way left, to conquer, but to flye.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Heroic Soul! Stay! This confirms me yours.
In quitting, you have gain'd me. I resolv'd
To make the utmost Tryal of your Faith,
And in your Faith of you. I've long in private
Weigh'd your Belief. I find by you 'tis Heavenly:
You've prov'd the practice; and 'twas a blest Vision
Bespoke my Change, no fickleness of Mind.
Whom shou'd I love indeed but him I've sworn to wed,
Who freed my Brother, and retreives my Soul!
Heav'n, Reason, Duty, Gratitude, and Love decree it,
Your Faith and you for ever, now are mine.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Amazement! Ravishment! am I awake!
And are you mine! I will, I must believe it.
Oh happy Change! O unexpected Bliss.
Look down, ye Sacred Choirs, and share my Joys,
While thus I pay my Thanks.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Nay, start not, take my Confirmation too.
I promis'd you to let Quisara's Hand
Be joyn'd with yours, and here I ratifie it.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Ha! Did I plot for this!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh! Thought is drown'd in Joy. How shall I speak my Thanks!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Hold, as the Gods have seen me just to you,
To the^r own Altars they must see me just.
Guards, seize your Prisoner—

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: That's well retriev'd! Be sure you bind him fast.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Is this your gratitude?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Bind your Restorer, Sir?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Oh Sister, with Reluctance I'm severe.
Had he offended me, I had forgiven,
But to our Gods the injury is done,
Blasphem'd, Revil'd: Yet still he may be yours,
He must appease our Gods by humble Worship,
Or fall a Sacrifice where he blasphem'd 'em;
And sure to save his Life, and gain you, he'll submit.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To serve my Princess, to secure my Joys
I'd rush thro' Seas, thro' Fires, I'd smile at danger,
I wou'd do any thing, but injure Heaven,
And to serve Idols were the greatest wrong.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What means my Friend? sure you'll not lose your self,
Oh quick, recant, submit, appease our Gods
And those more angry Men that awe me, and the People.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: He instantly must own our Gods or die.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What, use my breath t' abjure the Pow'r that gave it,
Renounce, th' Almighty Being! Worship Hell!
No more; bring me to Torments, Racks, and Fires;
I'll offer there my self: But when I quit my Faith,
And grow unworthy thus of her and mercy,
Let me dread ev'ry Curse that guilt deserves,
Want, Shame, Diseases, and what's worse, her hate,
Despair on Earth, and worse Despair below.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Mildness but hardens him. Our Bramins here demand him.
This Temple has its Prison; there they best
Will work the wish'd-for Change.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You're wise and holy:
Act for the best, but still respect my Friend.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Fear not. Death's no misusage of a Rival.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh, Sir, do not resign him to his Foes.
Rather exert your Pow'r. O save him, save your Friend.
I know he'll ne're abjure his Faith.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Then he must die.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: He shall not die! Oh! Sir, why turn you from me?
See, on her knees your Sister begs his Life;
With tears she begs it, save the Man that freed you,
Him I must wed, and wed by your command.
Must I bring on his death? O spare him! Father, holy men,
Joyn, joyn with me: True Piety is mild.
Oh whither wou'd you lead him! stay! stay! Take me too.
I'll not out live his Loss. No, I'll now save his Life,
Or lose my own. Our Love and Faith are one:
Our Fates must be the same.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How's this, Quisara!

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: She raves.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: No, thou false Man, like him I serve a Pow'r
That gives me strength to scorn your cursed Idols.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Ha! own his Faith.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I do, I do! Oh spare him! spare your Sister!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O fatal found.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Take him away, he hardens her in Error:

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh Princess!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: O Sir, will you then let him go? call, call him back!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O Sister! have a care, lose not your self; he will recant.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh never, Sir; ev'n I wou'd not to save him.
Then save us both. Nay, do not, do not fly me.
My hopes are all in you. Oh! hear me, hear me!
Let not blind Zeal prevail! save your own honour,
Can you resign us to be Butcher'd, mangled,
Our Limbs torn, and abandon'd to vile wretches?
Your dearest Friend, your Sister! sure you cannot.
Our hearts are near akin, and mine wou'd bleed
To see you thus distress'd. Thus I bore your affliction.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Oh I shall lose the Monarch in the Friend.
Rise, rise, Quisara.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh Sir!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Sister!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Brother! Friend!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Let Crowns be lost, and let me save my Sister and my Friend.
Thus in my arms, thus let me ever guard 'em.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Ha! all goes ill. Run, Call the Bramins hither.
Hope not to save 'em, tho' you lose your Crown.
No, King, the Gods can punish them and you.
Nay, if you pause, I've Judgments to denounce
From angry Heaven. The Sacred Choir attends;
Leave her to us, we'll only fright and preach her from her Errors —
Or put it past your Power to save her or my Rival.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh, King, do you then yield me up! Hold, wretches;
Touch not my hand. I'll freely go to Dungeons,
Nay, death it self, for such a Noble Cause:
Tho' Earth forsakes us, heaven will mend our Fates.
And pour severest Vengeance on your heads.
Yes, cruel men, then tremble, fear its anger,
Dread, dread its fierce Revenge! our blood will claim it.
But hold! we ought to love our very Foes.
Then Bless these Men: thou power of mercy, spare e'm.
May they like me their Idol Gods despise,
And dare to fall, more gloriously to rise.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I fear you'll not prevail. Oh urge not then
The Vengeance of the Gods too far: for if you do—

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: To clear your doubts we'll move the angry Powers
By solemn Incantation.

prose:
An Incantation set by Mr. D. and Purcell.

"HEar thou by whom the rattling Thunder's hurl'd!
"Hear, Parent Sun, bright Eye, and Monarch of the World.


Hear, gentle Moon, pale Queen of Night,
And ye refulgent Orbs of Light,
Great Court of Heaven so ample and so high,
And all ye swarming Commons of the Sky.




O Skies! O Sea! O Earth! on all Your Pow'rs call


E're the Blasphemers fall,


Oh hear our solemn call.




Hear, ye friendly earthly Powers,
Gods of kindly Fruits and Flowers,
Who, unseen, delight to trip
Where Birds flutter, hop, and skip,
Where there warble, chirp and coo,
Where in Whispers Zephirs woo,
Where poor Eccho sweetly grieves,
And remurmurs thro' the Leaves.




Rouse, ye Gods of the main!
Take Vengeance on those who your Altars prophane.
Hush no more the loud Storms! Command them to blow,
Till foaming with Rage the Waves roar as they flow,
"While they heave and they swell,
"Toss the Slaves to the Skies, and then plunge 'em to hell.


Infernal Pow'rs, grim sullen sprights
Who fill our Souls with dire affrights!
By all the dismal yell,
And horrors of your hell,
Your dreadful Pleasure tell.

End with the Verse, Hear ye Gods of the main, &c.




The Gods are Sullen, and displeased. But see
The Ancient Seer, who oft declares their will.
Advance, wise Bramin, while by Pow'r of sound,
We Prompt some God, by Thee to 'inform a Doubting Monrach.

verse:
OH Cease, cease, urge no more the God to swell my Breast!
The Mansion dreads the greater Guest.
But lo! he comes! I shake! I feel, I feel his Sway,
And now he hurries me along.
Then, Crouds, believe, and, Kings, obey,
'Tis Heav'n inspires the Song.


Haste! To the Gods due Vengeance give.
Hark! From their Seats they cry,
Who lets Blasphemers live,
Shall by Blasphemers die.
Haste, haste, due Vengeance give.
"Let the Sound
"Eccho all around.
Haste, haste, due Vengeance give.
Beware! Ten thousand, thousand threatning Ills I see!
Invasions! Wars! Plagues! Ruin! Endless Woes!
Ah wretched Isle, I weep for Thee,
Save, save thy self, Resign the God's Blaspheming Foes.
Now, now the Thunder roars.
The Earth now groans and quakes.
The rising Main a Deluge pours.
The World's Foundation shakes.
Hell gapes? The Fiends appear!
Oh hold, ye angry Pow'rs, relent, or we dispair.
See, we fulfill
On your Foes your dreadful Will.
See the Throng
Hoot 'em, as they're dragg'd along.

Now they tear 'em, now they dye;
All applaud, and shout for Joy.
Peace returns, all Nature smiles,
Happy Days now bless our Isles,
Now we laugh with Plenty crown'd,
Merry Sports and Love go round. —

"The Vision's o'er! — The God deserts my Brest.
"Hush! gently bear me hence to Rest.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now, Sir, you've heard the Gods confirm their Doom.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: They yet may Change.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: It must be quickly then.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: I'll try to win 'em. —

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Leave us to do that.
We dare not trust your Nature with the Parly.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Delay awhile.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Take heed! Dread, dread the Gods; if you defer their Doom.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Am I a King, and must they dye! my Sister, my Restorer!
Oh Death is in the Thought! First let it reach me.
Let Vengeance rage, and sweep me from the World, —
But Oh this will not save 'em. I must yield.
But judge my Grief, all great, all gen'rous Hearts!
Why do we boast of Pow'r? A Crown's a Pageant;
Kings are but glorious Slaves, controll'd by Odds,
The Priests, the People, and the greater Gods.
When These are touch'd, 'tis They the Scepter Weild,
And Kings, those petty Substitutes, must yield.
Empire's a stinted Grant, a Taste of Pow'r,
And we but Rule to feel Restraint the more.
Gods, do us right: 'Tis Just we be withstood
When doing Ill, but not when doing Good.

speeches.speaker: Quisara.
verse: HOW blest is Piety! It cheers my Soul,
Ev'n here, where I'm preparing for my Fate,
Of all but you forsaken! — Do not Weep;
You break my Peace of Mind, — Nay, then I beg,
I must not now Command, retire a while —
Grief is Infectious,— Now I think on them,
On my Distress, and poor Armusia, Doom'd
For me to fall, I Weep,—
Hark! The Bell tolls again! Our fatal Hour is come.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh my rack'd Soul! How shall I stand this Sight,
The strongest Tryal they cou'd put me to! Oh!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Ha! Whence that Groan?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh Princess!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh Armusia!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: How shall I dare t'approach that Suff'ring Vertue!
And yet I must. Thus then, now let me crawl,
And in this Agony breathe out a Soul
Rack'd with unutterable Love and Woe.

speeches.speaker: Qui
verse: Oh 'tis too much, thou best, thou only Lover,
Thou Lover of my Soul. I only greive for thee.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: And shall I not Grieve for you, betray'd for me to Death?
Not Grieve to see you here! Oh! Hopes of Heav'n,
'Tis only you ^n buoy. up sinking Vertue,
When such a Tryal comes. Let Pagan Fiends
On Racks Distend me, Burn me, Tear my Limbs,
I'd Smile, so you be safe. They cannot hurt me;
But when they Pain you, then my Heart they'll Tear.
Oh! at the Thought I shake, I bleed, I rave, and I dispair.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: I Glory in my Fate; then calm thy mind,
Dear Man; I've only Tears to pay thy Worth,
But we shall meet in Heav'n at better Nuptials,
There no bad Men shall interrupt our Joys.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh now you've rais'd my Soul from one Extream to t'other.
I dare Rejoyce ev'n here.

speeches.speaker: Officer.
verse: I'm bid to tell you, You must now attend
T'appease our Gods, or Dye. 'Tis the last Summons.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: We come.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To Dye.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: To Triumph.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Yes, my Bride.
But, sure I first may claim a Chaste Endearment
Due to a Bridegroom, and a Dying Friend.
Yes, blushing Saint, and thus I seize the Blessing,—
My Soul is on the Wing to mix with Thine;
Another Kiss, and they'd for ever joyn.
Oh! since below we taste such Sweets in Love,
How great, how vast must be our Joys above!

speeches.speaker: King
verse: OH! yet delay your Pious Cruelty.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: It makes me Weep to urge their Punishment,
But ev'n your Crown's at stake, if 'tis deferr'd.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: They come. I dread the Sight, yet still must try to win 'em.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I force my self to see you thus, to save you.
Sister, Armusia, Oh, once more I beg, —
Save, save your Lives.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Name not these Toys, when Heav'n's concern'd; For that, Sir,
I cou'd forego ev'n her, and yet what's Life without her?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: And I shou'd hate him, cou'd he love me more.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: Oh quick worship our Gods.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Oh Princess. —

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: No more.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Away, deluding Men.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: Your Life, —

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Take it, Bramin.
And all the Misery that shall attend it.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: Make the Fires ready.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Heav'n gives us Strength to dread 'em not.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Yet, Stay.
What shall I do to save you, Stubborn Pair?
Look on me, like the Criminal I beg,
And Majesty is fled from me, to you.
Why will you Kill me? Or, what's worse than Death,
Afflict me thus? Oh you've no Pangs to dread
More painful than I suffer. O submit —

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Save your mistaken Pity for your self, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bra.
verse: They must Dye instantly, they'll pervert all else.
You see all's ready, Sir, then pray retire,
Or we must Strike before your Eyes.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: 'Tis hard, ye injur'd Powers! Must I permit you Justice?
Oh Sister —

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Come, Grieve not, Sir! you wound my tender Soul.
Farewel. And may our Deaths instruct you how to Live.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Amazing Love, and Fortitude, and Zeal!
And shall I let you Dye!
Such Vertue, sure, deserves a better Fate.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: Arm, Sir! Seek for Defence. The Portuguese
Fire from their Fort and Ships upon the Town.
Gen'ral Ruidias sent t'inform us now
He'll Beat it down, unless Armusia be set Free.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Hah! Dares he do't? Must In-mates too Controul us?
Ev'n in this Case I must Resent th'Insult;
And, were I Rash, I wou'd Revenge it here.
However, bear 'em back to Prison, Guards:
And you demand a Parley.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Curst Event! Had now my Rival Fall'n,
I'd yet found means to save her.
BLess us, what Thundering's here, what Fire-spitting.
And how the Guns take the side of a House here, and the side of a House there, and mend them up again with another Ward.
I had the Roof of my House taken off with a Chain Shot, and in the twinkling of an Eye another clap't in the place on't.
That's a Gun I'll Swear.
You think he Lyes now, I ha' seen a Steeple taken off with a Chain Shot, and another put in the place on't, with Twenty Men Ringing the Bells.
Pish, what's that! I saw an Old Man's Head set upon a Young Man's Shoulders. —

But, Woe be to the Potters, I saw a Hand-Granado in one of their Shops, just now, and the Pots, Pans, Pipkins, and Glasses, at Fisticuffs with it, at such a rate, you'd ha' Sworn, a whole Troop of Devils had been at Foot-Ball there.
For my part, I'm afraid we shall all find ourselves Knock'd o'th He^d to Morrow Morning, as soon as we are awake.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Like enough.

They've rid me of as good a Wife as a Man wou'd desire to part withall. I met a Hand with a Letter in't just now in post haste, and by and by Whiz comes the Leg after it, as if the Hand had forgot half it's Errand.
Ay. I saw the very Man that had lost these Goods, come Hopping upon his t'other Leg that was left, to raise a Hue and Cry after the Bullet that had Robb'd him of half himself.

Wh^, d'ye think there's any Law for these Cannon Bullets then? 1. Law! No. Prethee run to a Granado when it comes Piping Hot out of a Mortar-piece, and tell't you'll take the Law of him. — I do but think what Lane a Ch^in-shot wou'd make in the Law, and how like an Ass a Judge wou'd sit on the Bench with his Head shot off.
I must confess, to have one's Head shot off, wou'd put any man out of Countenance.

A Friend of mine lost his Head just now, a very Honest Fellow, a Taylor, and 'twas no sooner off, but a Lawyer's Head that no body own'd, dropt out of the Clouds, and settled upon honest Stiche's Shoulders; the Fellow's Ruin'd by't — for he never spoke a True Word since.
What shall we do?

Let's to the King in a Body, all and one, and desire him to Compound with the Foe for such Lambs as we want most in our Callings. — Let me see, Thou ar^ a Fencer, thou shalt give thy Legs to secure thy Arms. Thou'rt a Dancer, thou shalt giue thy Head to secure thy Heels.
Thou'rt a Cuckold, thou shalt give thy Horns to secure thy Head.
Lets about it instantly, and go to the King.
Aye, so he is not where the Bullets fly. If he be, I must desire his Majesty to come to me.

speeches.speaker: Omn.
verse: Agreed, agreed.
What's the matter, now.—
Oh I am Slain, let me be carried off quickly, before I come to my self, for I cannot indure to be Shot to Death, as I am a living Man.

segments.head: ACT V. | SCENE. A Field or broad place near the Fort.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How dare you offer to prescribe us Laws
Proud Portuguese, and thus abuse the Liberty
My Predecessors gave you to fix here?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Thrice in my Prince's Name I sent to claim Armusia,
And Thrice you by your Priests sent word you scorn'd the Summons.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: That was my work.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Ha! Did they dare do this? Abuse my Name?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Nay, then I must be quick. Despair assist me.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Once more I claim him as my Prince's Subject.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Our Priests too claim him from our injur'd Gods,
He's Doom'd by them to Dye, nay, ev'n his Bride my Sister.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Curs'd are the Mouthes that doom'd 'em! Quickly save 'em.
I'll hearken to no Terms till they're deliver'd:
Ev'n you should pray me to do you that Justice,
I'll pay the Debt of Honour, which I owe him,
Do you the like, Sir, nor be still Deluded.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: But, Oh the Priests, the People!

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: The People, Sir, beg they may both be spar'd.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Then leave me, Sir, to take 'em from their Foes.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I can no longer what I wish oppose.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Help, help!

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Be dumb, or this shall make you so — be kind;
I'm not the old Drone you think.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: O why d'you drag me thus? hold.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I come not here to talk. I ev'n want Time
To seek out my curst Rival, and with This—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ha! Villan!

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Art thou here?

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh save your self and me, run, call for help.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Hold, if thou stir'st, I strike.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh Misery, oh horror!

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Stay, I'll ease thee.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Help, Murther, help.

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Ha! Monster! Seize him — how! The Treach'rous Governor!

speeches.speaker: King
verse: What do I see! my cruel Enemy!

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: Art thou a Prophet?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Curst Fortune!

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Blest deliverance!

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Surprising Change!

speeches.speaker: King
verse: How have I been abus'd! ye gen'rous Souls,
You've half perswaded me t'embrace your Faith.
You're free. Be happy now. Haste to the Pallace,
Let Sports and Mirth Revive; Feasts, Revels, Masques.
Guards take that Fiend, and e're we punish him,
Let the Croud see their Prophet.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Confusion! Thirst of Revenge, and Frantic Love undo me.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: How shall I thank you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rui.
verse: I've scarce yet paid my debt, Sir.
Thank your own Virtue and my Death to hopes,
Dispair has murther'd Love. I still withstood your Right,
While Honour gave me leave. No more; let's to the King.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: O Princess still I doubt I dream,
I dare not yet trust Fortune.
Still as I reach my hand She draws back her's,
And snatches from me her deriding Favours.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Oh, trust my heart, brave Man, that tells me now we're blest.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I must be so, 'twere now a Sin to doubt it.
Yes, Pleasure comes too strong not to be real.
I want a Name to call this Blessing by.
Oh Fortune, like her Sex, is wisely coy,
And deals us Sorrow but to raise our Joy.

segments.head: ACT V. | The SCENE changes to a Palace.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Come all, and share my Joys, Peace Reigns, the People pleased,
I've punish'd my worst Foe, and sav'd the best of Friends.
Let Music now resound. Begin the Sports
To entertain our Court, while I and They,
Too full of our new Joys to relish others,
Look back with pleasing Horror on past dangers.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh! Sir! accept my silent gratitude, words were not made to speak a Joy like mine.
I cannot speak my Thanks.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Rise, you're excus'd from words,
You must have time to calm the stormy Bliss.
Then leave awhile this bright Assembly here
To Mirth and soft delights.
We'll ease with Talk our Pangs of Joy within.
Now spight of Subtle Foes all Danger's past,
And Heav'n on Vertue showrs Rewards at last.
